\chapter{At the Station, and When Things Go Wrong}
\label{ch:ur-at-the-station-and-when-things-go-wrong}
\hlchaptermodality{271}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can buy a ticket and ask when the next train leaves (ek ṭikaṭ dījiye, aglī gāṛī kab hai?), and say what went wrong (merā thailā kho gayā, merī gāṛī chhūṭ gaī).}

Complete UR-R271-at-the-station: buy a ticket, ask when, and say what went wrong.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{ایک} \ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{دیجیے} (ek ṭikaṭ dījiye)}{ایک ٹکٹ دیجیے (ek ṭikaṭ dījiye)}]{\ur{ایک} \ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{دیجیے} (ek ṭikaṭ dījiye) — at the ticket window}

\label{lesson:UR-C271-ek-tikat-dijiye}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}turn left\textquotedblright{}, politely. (\emph{bāeṅ muṛiye}.) Then \textquotedblleft{}a ticket\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{ṭikaṭ}.) At the window you ask for one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a ticket, please}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ایک} \ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{دیجیے۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ek ṭikaṭ dījiye.} — \textquotedblleft{}A ticket, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{دیجیے}} (\emph{dījiye}) is \textbf{\ur{دینا}} asked politely. The place goes in front with \textbf{\ur{کا}} (\emph{kā}):

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{لاہور} \ur{کا} \ur{ایک} \ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{دیجیے۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Lāhaur kā ek ṭikaṭ dījiye.} — \textquotedblleft{}A ticket to Lahore, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{کتنے} \ur{کا} \ur{ہے؟}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ṭikaṭ kitne kā hai?} — \textquotedblleft{}How much is the ticket?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{کتنے} \ur{کا}} (\emph{kitne kā}), \textquotedblleft{}of how much\textquotedblright{}, asks a price.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: when does it leave?}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{اگلی} \ur{گاڑی} \ur{کب} \ur{ہے؟}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{aglī gāṛī kab hai?} — \textquotedblleft{}When is the next train?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{گاڑی}} (\emph{gāṛī}) is feminine, so \textbf{\ur{اگلی}} (\emph{aglī}), and so the future too:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{گاڑی} \ur{کتنے} \ur{بجے} \ur{جائے} \ur{گی؟}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{gāṛī kitne baje jāe gī?} — \textquotedblleft{}What time will the train leave?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{وہ} \ur{چار} \ur{بجے} \ur{جائے} \ur{گی۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{voh chār baje jāe gī.} — \textquotedblleft{}It will leave at four.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}When is the next train?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{aglī gāṛī kab hai?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}When is the next bus?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{aglī bas kab hai?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}When is the next taxi?\textquotedblright{} — \emph{aglī ṭaiksī kab hai?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}A ticket, please\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ur{ایک} \ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{دیجیے}}.) \textquotedblleft{}How much is it?\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{کتنے} \ur{کا} \ur{ہے؟}}) Why \textbf{\ur{اگلی}}? (\textbf{\ur{گاڑی}} is feminine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{چھوٹنا} (chhūṭnā)}{چھوٹنا (chhūṭnā)}]{\ur{چھوٹنا} (chhūṭnā) — to be missed, to be left behind}

\label{lesson:UR-C271-chhutna}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say \textquotedblleft{}when is the next train?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{aglī gāṛī kab hai?}) Then \textquotedblleft{}small\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{chhoṭā}.) Keep that word in mind.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{چھوٹنا}}
\textbf{\ur{چھوٹنا}} — \emph{chhūṭnā} — \textquotedblleft{}to be missed; to be left behind\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{گاڑی} \ur{چھوٹ} \ur{گئی۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{merī gāṛī chhūṭ gaī.} — \textquotedblleft{}I missed my train.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Word for word, \textquotedblleft{}my train got left behind\textquotedblright{}. The train is the subject, so \textbf{\ur{گئی}} (\emph{gaī}), feminine; you say nothing about yourself but \textbf{\ur{میری}}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{بس} \ur{چھوٹ} \ur{گئی۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{merī bas chhūṭ gaī.} — \textquotedblleft{}I missed my bus.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{چھوٹ}} (\emph{chhūṭ}) is spelled like \textbf{\ur{چھوٹا}} (\emph{chhoṭā}), \textquotedblleft{}small\textquotedblright{}, without its ending. Urdu leaves the vowel unwritten; the romanization tells them apart.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{چھوٹنا}} (\emph{chhūṭnā}) is inherited. CDIAL traces it to a reconstructed \emph{kṣuṭyate}, \textquotedblleft{}is released\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 3707), and lists its Hindi twin with the sense \textquotedblleft{}escapes\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chhūṭnā}, then \emph{merī gāṛī chhūṭ gaī}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I missed my bus\textquotedblright{} — \emph{merī bas chhūṭ gaī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{چھوٹنا}} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To be missed, to be left behind\textquotedblright{}.) \textquotedblleft{}I missed my train\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{گاڑی} \ur{چھوٹ} \ur{گئی}}.) And \textbf{\ur{چھوٹا}}? (\emph{chhoṭā}, \textquotedblleft{}small\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{حادثہ} (hādsā)}{حادثہ (hādsā)}]{\ur{حادثہ} (hādsā) — an accident}

\label{lesson:UR-C271-hadsa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say \textquotedblleft{}I missed my train\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{merī gāṛī chhūṭ gaī}.) Then \textquotedblleft{}a road\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{saṛak}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{حادثہ}}
\textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} — \emph{hādsā} — \textquotedblleft{}an accident\textquotedblright{}. It is masculine.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ایک} \ur{حادثہ} \ur{ہوا۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ek hādsā huā.} — \textquotedblleft{}There was an accident.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Word for word, \textquotedblleft{}an accident happened\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{\ur{ہوا}} (\emph{huā}), masculine.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{سڑک} \ur{پر} \ur{حادثہ} \ur{ہوا۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{saṛak par hādsā huā.} — \textquotedblleft{}There was an accident on the road.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} (\emph{hādsā}) is usually traced, through Persian, to Arabic \emph{ḥāditha}, \textquotedblleft{}an event\textquotedblright{}: something that happens. Its fourth letter is new to your hand; the next lesson takes it out.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hādsā}, then \emph{ek hādsā huā}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}There was an accident on the bridge\textquotedblright{} — \emph{pul par hādsā huā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}An accident\textquotedblright{}.) Why \textbf{\ur{ہوا}} and not \textbf{\ur{ہوئی}}? (\textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} is masculine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{ث} (se)}{ث (se)}]{\ur{ث} (se) — the letter inside \ur{حادثہ}}

\label{lesson:UR-W271-se}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ذ} once, and name it. (\emph{zāl}.)

Now say \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} (\emph{hādsā}), \textquotedblleft{}an accident\textquotedblright{}. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ث}}
\textbf{\ur{ث}} — \emph{se}, the sound \emph{s}, the same as \textbf{\ur{س}}.

It is the fourth letter of \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} (\emph{hādsā}). You already write \textbf{\ur{ت}}: \textbf{\ur{ث}} is that shape with \textbf{three dots} above it instead of two. Inside a word it is a single short tooth wearing the three dots. Urdu keeps it for words from Arabic.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ث}}
Put your pen on \ur{ث} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start this letter or which way to travel}. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} and point at \ur{ث} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ث} three times, saying \emph{s} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} once, joined, with three dots on the tooth
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ث}? (\textbf{se}, \emph{s}.) What tells it from \ur{ت}? (Three dots, not two.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{حادثہ}}, \emph{hādsā}, \textquotedblleft{}an accident\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ur{کھو} \ur{گیا} (kho gayā)}{کھو گیا (kho gayā)}]{\ur{کھو} \ur{گیا} (kho gayā) — when things go wrong}

\label{lesson:UR-C271-kho-gaya}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I missed my train\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}there was an accident\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{merī gāṛī chhūṭ gaī}, \emph{ek hādsā huā}.) Then \textquotedblleft{}to lose\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{khonā}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: it got lost}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{تھیلا} \ur{کھو} \ur{گیا۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{thailā kho gayā.} — \textquotedblleft{}The bag got lost.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{تھیلا} \ur{کھو} \ur{گیا۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{merā thailā kho gayā.} — \textquotedblleft{}My bag got lost.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{کتاب} \ur{کھو} \ur{گئی۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{merī kitāb kho gaī.} — \textquotedblleft{}My book got lost.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

The lost thing is the subject, as in \textbf{\ur{گاڑی} \ur{چھوٹ} \ur{گئی}}: \textbf{\ur{گیا}} for the masculine \textbf{\ur{تھیلا}} (\emph{thailā}), \textbf{\ur{گئی}} for \textbf{\ur{کتاب}}. The stem with \textbf{\ur{گیا}} says it is gone, and no \textbf{\ur{نے}} comes in.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: telling someone}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{نے} \ur{پولیس} \ur{کو} \ur{بتایا۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{maiṅ ne polīs ko batāyā.} — \textquotedblleft{}I told the police.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{تھانے} \ur{گیا۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{maiṅ thāne gayā.} — \textquotedblleft{}I went to the police station.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{جب} \ur{حادثہ} \ur{ہوا،}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{jab hādsā huā,}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{تو} \ur{ہم} \ur{سڑک} \ur{پر} \ur{تھے۔}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{to ham saṛak par the.} — \textquotedblleft{}When the accident happened, we were on the road.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}My bag got lost\textquotedblright{} — \emph{merā thailā kho gayā}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}My ticket got lost\textquotedblright{} — \emph{merā ṭikaṭ kho gayā}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}My book got lost\textquotedblright{} — \emph{merī kitāb kho gaī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}My bag got lost\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{تھیلا} \ur{کھو} \ur{گیا}}.) Does it take \textbf{\ur{نے}}? (No.) \textquotedblleft{}I told the police\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{نے} \ur{پولیس} \ur{کو} \ur{بتایا}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — at the station}

\label{lesson:UR-R271-at-the-station}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}how do you get to the station?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{isṭeshan kaise jāte haiṅ?}) Then \textquotedblleft{}turn left\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{bāeṅ muṛiye}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} A ticket to Lahore, please. How much is it?
  \item \emph{Say it:} When is the next train? It will leave at four.
  \item \emph{Say it:} I missed my train.
  \item \emph{Say it:} My bag got lost, and I told the police.
  \item \emph{Say it:} There was an accident on the road.
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ur{حادثہ}} once, and point at \ur{ث} inside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}A ticket, please\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ur{ایک} \ur{ٹکٹ} \ur{دیجیے}}.) Now the other way round: in \textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{گاڑی} \ur{چھوٹ} \ur{گئی}}, which word sets \textbf{\ur{گئی}}? (\textbf{\ur{گاڑی}}.) \textquotedblleft{}My book got lost\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{کتاب} \ur{کھو} \ur{گئی}}.) Which of these takes \textbf{\ur{نے}}: \textbf{\ur{کھو} \ur{گیا}} or \textbf{\ur{بتایا}}? (\textbf{\ur{بتایا}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
